title: Branching & Merging
summary: Branches are movable pointers, not copies of files — which is what makes them cheap. Learn how merges actually combine history, why conflicts happen, and how a branch can silently pick up the wrong changes.

slides.markdown:
Branching is the feature that makes git usable for real teams: dozens of people working on the same codebase without stepping on each other, each in their own line of history, merging back when ready.

The reason it's cheap enough to use constantly — create a branch per bug fix, per experiment, per five-minute idea — is that a branch costs almost nothing to create. It isn't a copy of your files; it's a single pointer, as covered in [Git's Mental Model](git-fundamentals-mental-model).

Merging is the other half: git has to reconcile two lines of history that diverged, and it does that with real logic, not just concatenation. Understanding that logic is what separates "I ran `git merge` and it worked" from actually knowing why a merge did what it did — and being able to fix it when it didn't.

slides.sectionTitle: A branch is a pointer, not a copy
slides.markdown:
Creating a branch (`git branch feature` or `git switch -c feature`) does not duplicate your files. It writes a 41-byte pointer into `.git/refs/heads/feature` holding the hash of your current commit. That's the entire operation — no file copying, no proportional-to-repo-size cost.

This is why git branches are near-instant regardless of repo size, while some older systems made branching an expensive, deliberate act (a real server-side copy). It changes the psychology of branching entirely: instead of one big branch per release, teams branch per task, per experiment, even per five-minute spike, because the cost of creating and discarding a branch is effectively free.

Switching branches (`git switch other-branch`) does touch your working directory — git has to update the files on disk to match the other branch's snapshot — but no new git objects are created by the switch itself, only by commits you make afterward.

```bash
git branch feature-x          # create a pointer at current commit, stay put
git switch feature-x          # move HEAD + working dir to that pointer
git switch -c feature-y       # create and switch in one step (recommended)
git checkout -b feature-y     # the older, pre-"switch" equivalent

git branch -d feature-x       # delete, but only if merged (safe)
git branch -D feature-x       # delete regardless of merge status (force)
```

`git switch` and `git restore` were split out of the overloaded `git checkout` specifically because `checkout` did too many unrelated things (switch branches, restore files, detach HEAD) and people confused them under pressure. Prefer `switch`/`restore` in anything you write today; `checkout` still works everywhere for compatibility and is what you'll see in older docs and muscle memory.

The `-d` vs `-D` distinction is a real safety rail: lowercase refuses to delete a branch with unmerged commits, so you get a warning instead of silently losing work that only existed on that branch.

slides.subTitle: Two entirely different operations behind one command
slides.markdown:
`git merge feature` does one of two very different things depending on the shape of history:

- **Fast-forward** — if `main` hasn't moved since `feature` branched off, `main`'s commits are a strict prefix of `feature`'s. Merging just slides the `main` pointer forward to `feature`'s tip. No new commit is created; history stays a straight line.
- **True three-way merge** — if `main` has *also* gained commits since the branches diverged, git can't just slide a pointer — both histories are real and need to be combined. Git creates a new **merge commit** with two parents, one from each branch tip.

The distinction matters because a fast-forward merge leaves no trace that a feature branch ever existed — the commits just appear to be on `main` directly. A true merge leaves a visible merge commit and a forked-then-rejoined shape in `git log --graph`. Teams that want every feature's boundary visible in history use `git merge --no-ff` to force a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible.

slides.subTitle: How git computes what changed on each side
slides.markdown:
Before combining two branches, git needs a reference point: the **merge base**, the most recent commit both branches share (found by walking each branch's parent chain until the paths meet — `git merge-base branch-a branch-b` shows it directly).

With that base, a merge is really a **three-way diff**: git computes what changed from base to `main`, and what changed from base to `feature`, then applies both sets of changes on top of the base. If the two sides touched different lines (or different files entirely), both changes apply cleanly and the merge auto-resolves. If both sides touched the **same lines**, git can't safely guess which version you want — that's exactly when you get a conflict.

This is worth internalizing over the popular but wrong shortcut of "merge just diffs the two tips against each other" — a two-way diff has no way to tell which side's change is the intentional new one, since it doesn't know what the base looked like.

```bash
$ git merge feature
Auto-merging config.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
```

Git leaves conflict markers directly in the file, for every hunk it couldn't resolve on its own:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30
=======
TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 45
>>>>>>> feature
```

Everything between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` is your current branch's version; everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>> feature` is the incoming branch's version. Resolving means editing the file to the content you actually want — delete the markers, keep one side, both, or something new entirely — then:

```bash
git add config.py       # marks this file's conflict as resolved
git commit               # completes the merge with a pre-filled message
```

`git status` mid-conflict lists every unresolved file explicitly, so you never have to guess what's left.

slides.sectionTitle: Merge commit vs squash vs fast-forward-only
slides.subTitle: What history each leaves behind
slides.markdown:
Three ways to land a feature branch, each producing a different shape in `main`'s history:

- **Merge commit** (`git merge`) — keeps every individual commit from the feature branch, plus one new two-parent merge commit. Full fidelity, noisier log.
- **Squash merge** (`git merge --squash`, or a PR platform's "squash and merge") — takes the *combined diff* of the whole branch and applies it as a single new commit on `main`, with no merge commit and no parent link back to the branch's individual commits. Clean, linear log; the original per-commit history only survives on the now-orphaned feature branch (or not at all, if it's deleted).
- **Fast-forward-only** (`git merge --ff-only`) — refuses to create a merge commit; if `main` isn't a strict ancestor of the branch, it errors out and asks you to rebase first. Produces a perfectly linear history, but demands rebasing before every merge.

There's no universally "correct" choice — it's a trade-off between preserving granular commit history (merge commit) and a clean, bisectable main-line log (squash or ff-only). Most teams pick one convention per repo and enforce it in the PR platform's settings rather than leaving it to individual judgment.

slides.subTitle: Integration pain scales with divergence
slides.markdown:
| | Long-lived feature branch | Short-lived feature branch |
|---|---|---|
| Typical lifespan | weeks to months | hours to a few days |
| Divergence from main | large — many commits on both sides | small |
| Conflict size when merged | large, often touching unrelated code | small, localized |
| Review size | huge PR, hard to review meaningfully | small PR, reviewable in one sitting |
| Failure mode | "merge day" becomes a dreaded event | merging is routine, low-stakes |

The mechanism behind this: conflict *likelihood and size* both scale with how much the two branches have independently changed since their merge base. A branch that lives two months while `main` gets 200 commits from everyone else is nearly guaranteed a painful reconciliation, regardless of how careful either side was.

This is the practical argument for trunk-based development and feature flags (covered in [Git Workflows & Collaboration](git-workflows-collaboration)): keep branches short, merge constantly, and hide unfinished work behind a flag rather than behind a long-lived branch.

`git merge feature` while standing on `main` merges `feature` **into** `main` — `main` gets a new merge commit, `feature` is untouched. Run it the other way around — checkout `feature`, then `git merge main` — and now `main`'s commits flow into `feature` instead, which is a completely different, and usually unintended, operation if you meant to update `main` with your feature's work.

The fix is always to check which branch you're currently on (`git branch` or your shell prompt) before merging — the direction is entirely determined by "what am I standing on," not by which two branch names you type.

slides.subTitle: A stale base hiding in a PR
slides.markdown:
A PR opened from a feature branch that hasn't pulled `main` in a while can show a "diff" full of changes the author never made — commits that landed on `main` from someone else, appearing to be part of the PR because the merge base is stale. Reviewers waste time re-reviewing code that's already on `main` and unrelated to the actual feature.

This happens because most PR tooling computes the diff against the **current merge base**, and if the feature branch is far behind `main`, that base is old — so the diff includes everything `main` gained in the meantime, not just what the feature branch actually changed.

The fix is to update the branch before opening or re-requesting review: `git rebase main` (rewrites the feature branch onto the latest main, covered in [Rebase vs Merge](rebase-vs-merge)) or `git merge main` into the feature branch. Either clears the phantom diff by moving the merge base forward to a recent commit.

slides.sectionTitle: What the merge algorithm can't know
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
Git's default merge strategy resolves conflicts **line by line**, with no understanding of the language it's merging. That has real limits worth naming out loud in an interview:

- **Semantic conflicts pass silently.** Two branches can each edit a *different* function in a way that's individually fine but breaks when combined — e.g. one branch renames a parameter, the other adds a call site using the old name. No text conflict occurs (different lines), yet the merged code doesn't compile or breaks at runtime. Line-based merging cannot catch this; only tests and CI can.
- **Rename detection is heuristic.** If one branch renames a file and the other edits its old path, git tries to detect the rename by content similarity and merge the edit into the new location — but below a similarity threshold, it treats them as unrelated add/delete, and you get a conflict or, worse, a silently dropped edit.
- **Whitespace and formatting churn amplify conflict surface.** A branch that reformats a whole file (even for good reasons, like running a linter) touches every line, which turns every subsequent merge against it into a conflict, even for unrelated one-line changes elsewhere in the file.

The practical takeaway: a clean merge is not proof of correctness, only proof that no two edits landed on the same lines. CI on the merged result is what actually validates the combination.

Merging doesn't just combine text — it combines *everything* on both sides, including a large binary or a secret that got committed on a branch by mistake. Once that branch merges into `main`, the object is reachable from `main` too, and every future clone of the repo pays for it forever, as covered in [Git's Mental Model](git-fundamentals-mental-model).

The merge-specific danger is that this can happen invisibly: a reviewer approving a 12-file PR diff isn't necessarily shown a 200 MB binary buried three commits back on the branch, because most review tools show the *combined* diff, not every intermediate commit. A pre-receive hook on the server (rejecting pushes over a size threshold, or files matching secret patterns) catches this before merge; reviewing only the final diff does not.
